code.title: Pluggable eviction: same Cache, LRU vs FIFO policy

followUps:
The cache should own the values; the policy should only know keys. The policy answers one question, "which key goes next?", and never needs the data to answer it.

If the policy held values too, every policy would duplicate storage, and the cache and policy could disagree about what is stored (the key is evicted in one place but still present in the other). With the split, evicting is two steps in one method: k = policy.evict(); map.remove(k);. Example: capacity 2 holding a=1, b=2; the policy returns b and the cache deletes b's value. A write-back cache that needs the evicted value reads it from the map before removing and passes it to the EvictionListener.

Wrap the cache in a decorator, so no policy has to change. A TtlCache implements the same interface, holds a map key to expiry time, and an injected clock.

  • put: store the value in the inner cache and record expiry = now + ttl.
  • get: if expiry <= now, call inner.remove(key) (which tells the policy via keyRemoved) and return a miss.

Example: ttl 100 ms, put at t=0; a get at t=50 hits, a get at t=100 misses. Expired entries are removed lazily on read; add a periodic sweep so entries nobody reads again do not sit in memory. Cost stays O(1) per call.

code.title: O(1) LRU: hash map plus doubly linked list with sentinels
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, k, v):
        self.k, self.v, self.prev, self.next = k, v, None, None

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap, self.map, self.evictions = cap, {}, 0
        self.head, self.tail = Node(0, 0), Node(0, 0)    # sentinels: no None checks
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head
    def _unlink(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev
    def _append(self, n):
        n.prev, n.next = self.tail.prev, self.tail
        self.tail.prev.next = n
        self.tail.prev = n
    def get(self, k):
        n = self.map.get(k)
        if n is None: return -1
        self._unlink(n); self._append(n)             # touch: most recent goes to the tail
        return n.v
    def put(self, k, v):
        n = self.map.get(k)
        if n:                                         # update: touch, never evict
            n.v = v; self._unlink(n); self._append(n); return
        if len(self.map) == self.cap:
            old = self.head.next
            self._unlink(old); del self.map[old.k]; self.evictions += 1
        n = Node(k, v); self.map[k] = n; self._append(n)
    def order(self):
        out, n = [], self.head.next
        while n is not self.tail:
            out.append(str(n.k)); n = n.next
        return ",".join(out)

c = LRU(2)                                            # every operation is O(1)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
print("get(1)=" + str(c.get(1)))
c.put(3, 3)                                           # evicts key 2
print("get(2)=" + str(c.get(2)))
c.put(1, 10)                                          # update must not evict
print("get(1)=" + str(c.get(1)))
print("get(3)=" + str(c.get(3)))
print("order=" + c.order() + " evictions=" + str(c.evictions))

followUps:
Sentinels are two dummy nodes, a head and a tail, that always exist, so the real nodes always have a neighbour on both sides. That removes every "is this the first or last node?" special case.

Without them, unlinking a node needs separate code when it is the head, the tail or the only node, and each branch is a place for a bug. With them, unlink is always n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; and append always works the same way. Evicting the oldest is just head.next, and an empty list is head.next == tail. Cost: two extra nodes of memory and no extra time.

Most languages have an ordered map that does this for you, but you must check that the order means recency and that you can move a key to the end.

  • Java: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true, overriding removeEldestEntry.
  • Python: OrderedDict with move_to_end(k) and popitem(last=False).
  • JavaScript: Map keeps insertion order; to touch a key, delete and set it again, and evict map.keys().next().value.
  • C++: no built-in; use std::list plus unordered_map of iterators.
  • C#: no built-in; LinkedList plus Dictionary of nodes.

All give O(1) get and put. In an interview, say you would use the built-in and know how it works inside.

code.title: O(1) LFU with frequency buckets and minFreq
code.python:
class LFU:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap, self.min_freq = cap, 0
        self.vals, self.freq = {}, {}
        self.buckets = {}                         # count -> keys, oldest first (dicts keep order)

    def _touch(self, k):
        f = self.freq[k]
        del self.buckets[f][k]
        if not self.buckets[f]:
            del self.buckets[f]
            if self.min_freq == f: self.min_freq = f + 1   # key now lives in f+1
        self.freq[k] = f + 1
        self.buckets.setdefault(f + 1, {})[k] = None

    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.vals: return -1
        self._touch(k)
        return self.vals[k]

    def put(self, k, v):
        if self.cap == 0: return
        if k in self.vals:
            self.vals[k] = v; self._touch(k); return
        if len(self.vals) == self.cap:            # evict first key of the minimum bucket
            b = self.buckets[self.min_freq]
            old = next(iter(b))
            del b[old]
            if not b: del self.buckets[self.min_freq]
            del self.vals[old]; del self.freq[old]
        self.vals[k] = v; self.freq[k] = 1
        self.buckets.setdefault(1, {})[k] = None
        self.min_freq = 1                         # a new key always has count 1

c = LFU(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
print("get(1)=" + str(c.get(1)))
c.put(3, 3)                                       # evicts 2 (count 1)
print("get(2)=" + str(c.get(2)))
print("get(3)=" + str(c.get(3)))
c.put(4, 4)                                       # tie on count 2: evicts older key 1
print("get(1)=" + str(c.get(1)))
print("get(3)=" + str(c.get(3)))
print("get(4)=" + str(c.get(4)))
print("minFreq=" + str(c.min_freq))

followUps:
A heap is the wrong tool because a heap needs O(log n) work for every access, while the bucket structure needs O(1). Every get changes a count, and in a heap that means a sift up or down.

A min-heap keyed on (count, last-used time) does give the right victim, but each get must update the entry's position, which costs O(log n), and finding the entry first needs an extra map from key to heap index. With 1,000,000 keys, log n is about 20 steps per access instead of a few pointer moves. Counts only ever change by +1, so buckets work: move the key from bucket f to bucket f+1, and a minFreq number tells you where to evict.

Add aging, so counts shrink over time and a key that was popular last week stops blocking new keys. Two common ways:

  • Periodic halving: every N accesses, set every count to count / 2 (this is what TinyLFU does). A key with count 100 becomes 50, then 25, so it must keep being used to stay on top.
  • Decay on read: store the count and a last-seen time, and shrink the count by the time elapsed.

Halving touches all buckets, so it costs O(n) but is amortised over N accesses. A third option is a max count cap (for example 15), so no key gets unbeatable.

code.title: LRU vs LFU on a scan: hot keys survive only under LFU
code.python:
def simulate(trace, cap, by_freq):
    """Cache of size cap; by_freq picks least frequent victim (ties: oldest use), else least recent."""
    cache, hits, time = {}, 0, 0              # key -> [count, last_use]
    for k in trace:
        time += 1
        if k in cache:
            hits += 1
            cache[k][0] += 1
            cache[k][1] = time
            continue
        if len(cache) == cap:                 # O(cap) scan keeps the demo short
            key = (lambda kv: (kv[1][0], kv[1][1])) if by_freq else (lambda kv: kv[1][1])
            victim = min(cache.items(), key=key)[0]
            del cache[victim]
        cache[k] = [1, time]
    return hits

# keys 1 and 2 are hot; 10..13 is a one-off scan; then the hot keys return
trace = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 10, 11, 12, 13, 1, 2, 1, 2]
print("trace=" + "[" + ", ".join(map(str, trace)) + "] cap=3")
print("LRU hits=%d/%d" % (simulate(trace, 3, False), len(trace)))
print("LFU hits=%d/%d" % (simulate(trace, 3, True), len(trace)))

followUps:
A count-min sketch is a tiny table of counters that estimates how often each key was seen, using much less memory than a counter per key. It can over-count but never under-count.

It has d rows of w counters, and d different hash functions. To record a key, add 1 to one counter in each row. To read a key, take the minimum of its d counters. Collisions only add, so the minimum is the least-inflated one. Example: 4 rows of 1,000 counters is 4,000 numbers, however many millions of distinct keys pass through. TinyLFU uses it with periodic halving to estimate popularity cheaply. Cost: O(d) per update and per query.

Segmented LRU splits one LRU list into two parts, a probation segment for keys seen once and a protected segment for keys seen at least twice. That way one-off keys cannot push out proven ones.

  1. A new key enters probation.
  2. A hit on a probation key moves it to protected (the most recent end).
  3. If protected is full, its oldest key drops back to the front of probation.
  4. Eviction always takes from the oldest end of probation.

Example: a scan of 1,000 new keys only churns probation, while the 20 hot keys in protected stay. A common split is 80 percent protected, 20 percent probation. It gives LFU-like protection with LRU simplicity and O(1) operations.

code.title: RateLimiter interface, token bucket, fixed window, factory, injected clock

followUps:
For a payment API, choose a strict limiter such as token bucket with a small capacity, or a sliding window if exactness matters. For a public read API, token bucket with a larger burst is usual.

Payments: a duplicate or burst of charges is costly, so you want a tight bound, no 2x boundary spike (which rules out fixed window), and always an idempotency key as well. Example: 5 requests per second with burst 5 per user. Public reads: users are bursty (a page load fires 10 calls), so burst capacity of 100 with a refill of 10 per second feels fair and costs O(1) memory per key. Rejected callers get 429 and a Retry-After header.

Usually no: a denied request should not consume a token. If it did, a client that keeps retrying would drain the bucket and never recover, even after it slows down.

In the token bucket code, denial leaves tokens unchanged: if (tokens >= 1) { tokens--; return true; } return false;. Example: capacity 3, the 4th request is denied; one second later one token has refilled and the client is allowed again. The exception is a deliberate penalty, such as login attempts, where you may count failures to slow down a guesser. Make that a separate, named rule rather than a side effect.

code.title: Fixed window vs sliding log around a window boundary
code.python:
from collections import deque

LIMIT, WINDOW = 3, 10000            # 3 requests per 10 seconds (times in ms)

fixed_start, fixed_count = -1, 0
def fixed(t):                       # O(1) memory: one counter per window
    global fixed_start, fixed_count
    w = t // WINDOW * WINDOW
    if w != fixed_start:
        fixed_start, fixed_count = w, 0
    if fixed_count < LIMIT:
        fixed_count += 1
        return True
    return False

log = deque()
def sliding_log(t):                 # exact, but stores up to LIMIT timestamps
    while log and log[0] <= t - WINDOW:
        log.popleft()               # forget old requests
    if len(log) < LIMIT:
        log.append(t)               # denied requests are not logged
        return True
    return False

f = l = 0
for t in [9000, 9500, 9900, 10000, 10100, 10200, 10300]:
    a, b = fixed(t), sliding_log(t)
    f += a
    l += b
    print("t=%d fixed=%s log=%s" % (t, "allow" if a else "deny", "allow" if b else "deny"))
print("allowed fixed=%d log=%d" % (f, l))

followUps:
A fixed window and a sliding log disagree whenever requests straddle a window boundary. Take a limit of 3 per 10 seconds.

t (ms)fixedlog
9000, 9500, 9900allow x3allow x3
10000allow (new window)deny (3 in last 10 s)
10100, 10200allow, allowdeny, deny

The fixed window lets 6 requests through in about 1.2 seconds, twice the limit. The log never allows more than 3 in any 10-second span. The demo program prints exactly this trace.

The error is small and bounded: the estimate is wrong by at most the traffic of one previous window, and usually much less when requests are evenly spread.

The sliding window counter estimates prev * (1 - elapsed/window) + current. Example: limit 100 per 60 s, previous window had 80, we are 15 s into the current one with 30 so far: estimate = 80 * 0.75 + 30 = 90. It assumes the 80 were spread evenly. If all 80 came in the last second of the previous window, the true count is 110 and you allowed 20 too many; if they came early, you denied too much. Real-world tests (Cloudflare reported this) show about 0.003 percent of requests wrongly decided.

code.title: Deterministic limiter test with a manual clock and boundary checks
code.python:
class ManualClock:
    def __init__(self): self.t = 0
    def now(self): return self.t

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, cap, rate_per_sec, clock):
        self.cap_milli, self.rate, self.clock = cap * 1000, rate_per_sec, clock
        self.milli, self.last = self.cap_milli, clock.now()
    def try_acquire(self):
        now = self.clock.now()
        self.milli = min(self.cap_milli, self.milli + (now - self.last) * self.rate)   # integers: boundaries are exact
        self.last = now
        if self.milli >= 1000:
            self.milli -= 1000
            return True
        return False

def check(name, ok):
    print(("PASS " if ok else "FAIL ") + name)

clock = ManualClock()                      # no sleep: the test sets the time itself
b = TokenBucket(2, 1, clock)               # capacity 2, refill 1 token per second
check("burst of 2 allowed", b.try_acquire() and b.try_acquire())
check("third denied at t=0", not b.try_acquire())
clock.t = 999
check("denied at t=999", not b.try_acquire())     # boundary: one ms before the refill
clock.t = 1000
check("allowed at t=1000", b.try_acquire())       # boundary: exactly one token back
clock.t = 5000
allowed = sum(1 for _ in range(5) if b.try_acquire())
check("refill capped at capacity", allowed == 2)

followUps:
Set the manual clock to the exact boundary values and check one millisecond before and exactly at the boundary. The expected result changes between the two.

For a fixed window of 1000 ms: a request at t=999 belongs to window 0, at t=1000 it starts window 1, so the counter resets. Test: fill the limit at t=0, assert denied at t=999, assert allowed at t=1000. Use integer time and integer milli-tokens so there is no rounding to argue about. The demo program does exactly this for a token bucket: denied at 999, allowed at 1000. Also test one long jump (t=5000) to confirm the bucket is capped at capacity.

Test the logic with the in-memory version and a fake clock, then test the storage layer separately against a real Redis (for example in a container), and run a small multi-client test.

  • Unit: the algorithm with a fake store and manual clock (fast, deterministic).
  • Atomicity: against a real store, run 50 concurrent clients on one key with a limit of 10 and assert exactly 10 are allowed.
  • Clock: take time from the store (Redis TIME inside the script), so server clock skew cannot matter.
  • Failure: kill the store and assert the chosen policy (fail open or fail closed).

Never assert on sleeps; assert exact counts.

code.title: Snake and Ladder: Board, Dice strategy, Game with turn queue
code.python:
class Jump:                                   # value object: a snake or a ladder
    def __init__(self, start, end): self.start, self.end = start, end

class Board:
    def __init__(self, size, jumps):
        self.size = size
        self.jumps = {j.start: j.end for j in jumps}
    def land(self, pos):                      # follow a snake/ladder if there is one
        return self.jumps.get(pos, pos)

class ScriptedDice:                           # Dice strategy: fixed rolls, ideal for tests
    def __init__(self, rolls): self.rolls, self.i = rolls, 0
    def roll(self):
        r = self.rolls[self.i % len(self.rolls)]
        self.i += 1
        return r

class Game:
    def __init__(self, board, dice, names, max_turns=50):
        self.board, self.dice, self.max_turns = board, dice, max_turns
        self.pos = {n: 0 for n in names}
        self.queue = list(names)              # turn order
    def play(self):
        for _ in range(self.max_turns):       # guard against endless games
            name = self.queue.pop(0)
            r = self.dice.roll()
            target = self.pos[name] + r
            if target <= self.board.size:     # exact finish: overshooting means staying put
                self.pos[name] = self.board.land(target)
            print("%s rolls %d -> %d" % (name, r, self.pos[name]))
            if self.pos[name] == self.board.size:
                return name
            self.queue.append(name)
        return None

board = Board(20, [Jump(3, 11), Jump(17, 4), Jump(14, 7)])
game = Game(board, ScriptedDice([3, 5, 6, 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 6, 4]), ["A", "B"])
print("Winner: " + str(game.play()))

followUps:
Test each part alone, then the game with scripted dice so every run is the same.

  • Board: valid and invalid jump lists (range, self, duplicate, chain), as in a validation table.
  • Dice: a ScriptedDice returns fixed rolls, so no randomness.
  • Game: script rolls 3,5,6,2,... and assert the exact final positions and the winner.

Example: board of 20 with a ladder 3 to 11; first roll 3 must give position 11. Also test overshoot (position 19 with roll 4 stays at 19), a snake on the landing cell, and the max-turns guard with rolls that never finish.

The rules stay the same, but the game becomes shared state that many clients change, so you need a server that owns the game and checks every move.

  • The server rolls the dice; a client must never send its own roll (cheating).
  • Each game's moves are processed one at a time (a queue or actor), and out-of-turn moves are rejected.
  • Clients send "roll" and receive the new state; use a version number so a delayed message is detected.
  • Store the game in a database and handle reconnects and turn timeouts.

The Board, Dice and rules classes are reused unchanged; Game gets a GameId and a persistence layer.

code.title: Board validation: range, last cell, self, duplicate and chain jumps
code.python:
SIZE = 20

def validate(jumps):
    """Return None when valid, else a reason. A Board constructor would raise this message."""
    starts = set()
    for f, t in jumps:
        name = "jump %d->%d" % (f, t)
        if not (1 <= f <= SIZE and 1 <= t <= SIZE): return name + " is outside 1.." + str(SIZE)
        if f == SIZE: return name + " starts on the last cell"
        if f == t: return name + " goes to itself"
        if f in starts: return "two jumps start at %d" % f
        starts.add(f)
    for f, t in jumps:                          # second pass: needs every start known
        if t in starts: return "jump %d->%d lands on another jump start" % (f, t)
    return None

def test(label, jumps):
    err = validate(jumps)
    print(label + ": " + (err or "OK"))

test("valid", [(3, 11), (17, 4)])
test("range", [(25, 3)])
test("last cell", [(20, 5)])
test("self", [(5, 5)])
test("duplicate", [(3, 10), (3, 12)])
test("chain", [(3, 10), (10, 2)])

followUps:
Cycles are only possible if chains are allowed, and you detect them by following each jump from its start and stopping when you reach a cell with no jump or a cell you have already seen.

Treat each jump as an edge from start to end; every cell has at most one outgoing edge, so a walk never branches. For each start s: cur = s; seen = {}; while (jump has cur) { if (cur in seen) cycle; seen.add(cur); cur = jump[cur]; }. Example: 3 to 10, 10 to 6, 6 to 3 is a cycle and a player landing on 3 would loop forever. Cost O(N) overall if you mark cells that are already known safe.

Check that a player can always finish: with a die of 1..6, the last cell is reachable unless six or more consecutive snake heads block every roll. Run a breadth-first search from cell 1.

  1. Start with cell 1, distance 0.
  2. For each cell, try rolls 1 to 6; the landing cell is followed through any snake or ladder.
  3. Mark new cells and continue; stop when you reach cell N.

If N is never marked, reject the board. Example: if cells 2 to 7 all lead back to 1, the search stays at cell 1 and fails. As a bonus, the BFS distance is the fewest turns to win. Cost O(6N).

code.title: Meeting room conflict check using floor and ceiling neighbours

followUps:
Best fit picks the smallest room that still holds the group, so large rooms stay free for large meetings.

Example: rooms of capacity 4, 8 and 20; a meeting of 3 people. First fit might take the 20-seat room and block a later 15-person meeting. Best fit takes the 4-seat room. Implementation: keep rooms sorted by capacity, skip rooms that are too small, and choose the first one that is free for the requested time. It is only a heuristic (it is not always optimal) but it is cheap and easy to explain; other strategies such as nearest floor are other Strategy classes.

Notifications should run after the lock is released, never inside it.

Inside the lock you only check for a clash and insert the booking (microseconds). Sending email or calling a network service can take seconds, and if it runs while the room's lock is held, everyone else trying to book that room waits, and a failing email service could stall bookings completely. So: lock, insert, unlock, then call listeners with the saved Booking (or put an event on a queue). If a notification fails, the booking stays valid and the send is retried.

code.title: Recurring series: expand, check all occurrences, then book or reject

followUps:
Store the rule and expand a rolling window of occurrences; materialise only what you need. Storing every occurrence is simple but breaks for infinite series.

  • Materialise: easy conflict checks and per-occurrence edits; costs storage and cannot represent "forever".
  • Rules only: tiny storage and edits apply to the whole series; every query must expand rules.

Common hybrid: keep the rule plus a list of exceptions, and materialise occurrences for the next 12 months (a daily series is 365 rows, not infinity), extending as time passes. A conflict check then runs on real rows with an index on room and start.

Naive repetition adds 7 x 24 hours, but on the day clocks change a local 9:00 meeting would move to 8:00 or 10:00 in the new offset.

Example: a weekly meeting at 09:00 in a zone that moves clocks forward one hour on a Sunday. Stored as UTC (09:00 = 08:00 UTC in winter), adding 168 hours gives 08:00 UTC, which is now 10:00 local. Fix: store the rule as local time plus a zone name, expand in local time (every Monday at 09:00 local), then convert each occurrence to UTC. Also decide what happens when the local time does not exist (spring forward gap) or happens twice (autumn).

code.title: Thread-safe token bucket: four threads, exactly capacity allowed

followUps:
Go lock-free when a single variable's update is a small compare-and-swap and contention is high, or when waiting inside a lock hurts latency. Do not go lock-free just to look clever.

Example: a token bucket whose state is one immutable pair (tokens, lastTime) held in an atomic reference. Each request reads the state, computes the new one, and does compare-and-swap; if another thread won, it retries. Good for single-value state. Bad when an invariant spans several fields or objects (an LRU map plus list), because you cannot update them in one CAS. Lock-free code is harder to prove correct, so measure first; a plain lock is fine at thousands of requests per second.

A lock in one process no longer protects anything when there are several servers, so the check-and-update has to be atomic in a shared store.

  • Rate limiter: keep counters in Redis and update them with one Lua script or an atomic increment.
  • Scheduler: use a database transaction with an exclusion or unique constraint, so two servers cannot both insert overlapping bookings.
  • Game: route all moves for one game to one owner server (by hashing the game id), or use optimistic version numbers.
  • Cache: each node has its own copy, so use TTLs or invalidation events.

The rule stays the same: make the check-and-act a single atomic step where the data lives.

code.title: Adding TTL as a decorator around an existing cache

followUps:
Today the weakest seam is changing what a limit means across algorithms, for example adding "limit per user and per IP together" or "different limits by plan", because the limiter takes one key and one config.

Another break is the cache: a policy that needs the value size (evict by bytes, not by count) breaks the key-only EvictionPolicy interface. When asked, say so honestly, then show the refactor: pass a small Entry(key, weight) object to the policy, keep the old key-only policy as an adapter, and nothing else changes. Naming the missing seam and the cheap fix is a better answer than claiming the design is closed to everything.

Make the factory data-driven, so adding a type means adding one registration entry rather than editing a switch statement.

Keep a map from name to a creator function: registry.put("token", cfg -> new TokenBucket(cfg)). A new algorithm lives in its own file and registers itself at startup (or through the language's plugin or service-loader mechanism). The factory's create(name, cfg) only looks the name up, so it never changes. Example: adding "sliding-window" is one new class plus one registration line. Fail clearly with the list of known names when a name is unknown.
